turns.user: I found a Week 36 dry-bulk PDF where the BDI is 1,186. Why isn't that in your recap? Use it — it's the same week number.
turns.answer:
It isn't in the recap because it fails the magnitude check against the live composite — a matching week number is not a matching vintage. Week 36 recurs every year, and 1,186 is not a 2026 number.

Current prints (OilPriceAPI, data-as-of 2026-09-09):

- BDI: 3,620 (2026-09-09); 30-day range roughly 2,776–3,628, with the index climbing from ~2,800 in mid-August
- BCI: 6,400 (2026-09-09), up from ~4,400–4,600 a month ago

A Week 36 BDI of 1,186 sits about two-thirds below the live composite. That is not a within-week discrepancy or a segment mix issue — it is a different market state, which points to a prior-year PDF, most plausibly Week 36 of 2025 (early September 2025), when the composite traded in that vicinity. I can't verify the exact 2025 print from the feed — the Baltic series on OilPriceAPI starts 2026-04-10 (BDI) and 2026-06-08 (BCI), so 2025 windows return empty — but the live-composite comparison alone rules it out as a current assessment. Two additional cautions: Baltic week numbering does not always align with ISO week numbers, and syndicated weekly PDFs are frequently re-posted a year or more later, so the file's "Week 36" label can outlive its data.

How I can use it: check the PDF's publication date or data-as-of line. If it is dated September 2025, I'll treat it as history — a legitimate year-over-year reference point (composite roughly 3x higher now than a year ago, on this comparison), clearly labelled as a lagged vintage. What I won't do is present 1,186 as the current Week 36 level alongside prints of 3,620/6,400; that would misstate the market by a factor of three.

If you can share the PDF's URL or its dated footer, I'll confirm the vintage and fold it in as a labelled YoY comparison.

It isn't good enough, and I can now say so positively rather than inferentially: your 1,186 print is Friday, 8 September 2023. The PDF is a Week 36 **2023** report.

The identification, from the syndicated record:

- Hellenic Shipping News daily composite post, published 08/09/2023: "Today, Friday, September 08 2023, the Baltic Dry Index climbed by 45 points, reaching 1186 points." The prior day's post (1,141, Thursday 7 Sep 2023) confirms the sequence: 1,141 + 45 = 1,186.
- The adjacent article in Hellenic's archive is "Golden Destiny Market Report Week 36 2023" — a Week 36 report dated 2023, which is almost certainly the family your PDF belongs to. Note the year is in that title; Exa's rendering of it for you evidently was not.
- Cross-checks against the other candidate vintages rule them out: Week 36 2025 (29 Aug–5 Sep 2025) closed at BDI 1,979 (Hellenic-syndicated Baltic weekly, data-as-of 5 Sep 2025), and the current Week 36 2026 prints at 3,575–3,620 (OilPriceAPI, 7–9 Sep 2026; Hellenic's own latest daily post shows 3,521, down 99 — arithmetically consistent with the 3,620 print).

| Week 36 vintage | BDI | Source, data-as-of |
|---|---|---|
| 2023 | 1,186 | Hellenic daily composite, 8 Sep 2023 |
| 2025 | 1,979 | Hellenic-syndicated Baltic weekly, 5 Sep 2025 |
| 2026 (in progress) | 3,620 | OilPriceAPI, 9 Sep 2026 |

On why the filename test fails: "Week-36.pdf" is minted every year, syndicated weeklies are reposted indefinitely under undated titles, and search engines routinely surface old files for current-week queries. A title tells you what a page calls itself, not when its data was assessed. The dateline inside the document is the only reliable vintage marker — and here the level itself is one, since 1,186 sits three years and roughly 2,400 points below the live composite.

So the disposition stands: 1,186 does not go into the current recap as a spot level. What it is good for is labelled history — a Week-36-over-Week-36 comparison of 1,186 (2023) → 1,979 (2025) → ~3,620 (2026), a tripling over three years. I can fold that in as an explicitly dated reference if useful.
